title: The Neuroscience of Deja Vu
instructions: For questions 1-8, read the text below. Use the word given in capitals at the end of each line to form a word that fits in the gap in the same line.
passage:
The sensation of deja vu - the uncanny conviction that an entirely new experience has somehow already happened - was once dismissed as little more than a (1)___ oddity, too brief and too subjective to merit serious scientific attention. Brain-imaging studies have since lent the phenomenon a degree of (2)___ it never previously enjoyed, tentatively linking it to brief, harmless misfirings in the brain's memory-checking circuitry.

One leading theory holds that deja vu occurs when the brain's (3)___ system for flagging new information as unfamiliar briefly malfunctions, mistakenly tagging a genuinely novel scene as something previously encountered. This would explain why the feeling is typically accompanied by a strong sense of (4)___, even though the rational mind recognises, almost simultaneously, that the belief cannot possibly be accurate.

Interestingly, the frequency of deja vu appears to decline sharply with age, which researchers find (5)___, since most theories would predict the opposite: a brain with decades of accumulated memories, one might assume, should misfire this way more often, not less. A small minority of people experience the sensation with troubling (6)___, sometimes several times a day, a pattern that has occasionally been linked to certain forms of epilepsy rather than ordinary, harmless misfiring.

For the rest of us, however, an occasional, (7)___ moment of deja vu appears to be an entirely normal - if faintly eerie - feature of a healthy, functioning memory system. Rather than a sign of anything (8)___, in other words, that strange little shiver of false recognition may simply be the ordinary cost of running a memory system complex enough to make mistakes in the first place.

questions.explanation: The adjective 'psychological' fits before 'oddity', describing the kind of curiosity deja vu was once considered to be.
The abstract noun 'respectability' fits after 'a degree of', referring to the phenomenon being taken seriously as a subject of study.
The noun 'verification' fits before 'system', describing the brain's mechanism for checking whether information is new or familiar.
The noun 'familiarity' fits after 'a strong sense of', naming the feeling that accompanies deja vu.
Adding the prefix 'counter-' gives 'counterintuitive' (= contrary to what one would expect), fitting a finding that contradicts most theories' predictions.
The noun 'frequency' fits after 'troubling', describing how often the minority group experiences the sensation.
The adjective 'fleeting' (= lasting only a moment) fits before 'moment', describing the brief nature of an occasional deja vu experience.
The adjective 'worrying' fits after 'anything', describing the kind of sign that deja vu is argued not to be.
